facts.claim: The mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance.
facts.quote: The results of the conducted experiment imply that the mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance, which supports the hypothesis of the smartphone presence using limited cognitive resources.

facts.claim: Interruptions coming early during a search task are more likely to result in the user forgetting the primary task goal than interruptions that arrive later on.
facts.quote: In addition, we show that interruptions coming early during a search task are more likely to result in the user forgetting the primary task goal than interruptions that arrive later on.
facts.causalWarning: causal wording, but the cited study only shows an association

facts.claim: There is a general tendency to resume tasks, but no memory advantage for unfinished tasks.
facts.quote: We found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks but found a general tendency to resume tasks.

facts.claim: Notifications are more disruptive for fast, stimulus-driven search tasks than for slower, more effortful semantic-based search tasks.
facts.quote: Our findings replicate earlier work, showing the generally harmful effects of IM, and further show that notifications are more disruptive for fast, stimulus-driven search tasks than for slower, more effortful semantic-based search tasks.

facts.claim: When the primary task was considered difficult, subjects forced to multitask had significantly lower performance compared with not only the subjects who did not multitask but also the subjects who were able to multitask at their discretion.
facts.quote: The results show that when the primary task was considered difficult, subjects forced to multitask had significantly lower performance compared with not only the subjects who did not multitask but also the subjects who were able to multitask at their discretion.

facts.claim: Reducing notification-caused interruptions is beneficial for performance and reducing strain.
facts.quote: The findings revealed that a reduction of notification-caused interruptions is beneficial for performance and reducing strain.

research.angle: While notifications cause measurable performance drops and strain, their impact varies depending on task difficulty, the timing of the interruption, and the mere presence of a device.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that notifications and the presence of smartphones disrupt cognitive performance and memory, though the severity depends on the specific nature of the task being performed.
research.caveat: The research does not fully explain the specific role of anxiety in impeding performance when notifications are disabled.
